title: Why language models hallucinate
summary: Surveys split hallucination into factuality and faithfulness types and list causes in data, training and generation, including sampling for diversity.

beats.say: A language model can state a false fact in a confident tone.
Researchers call this hallucination, and split it into two types.
Factuality hallucination: the output diverges from verifiable real world facts.
Faithfulness hallucination: the output diverges from the user's input, or from itself.
The survey lists causes in the data, in training, and at generation time.
In the data: misinformation and biases in the pretraining text.
In training, tuning on knowledge the model does not have is a listed cause.
At generation time, decoding choices and over-confidence add to it.
An earlier survey adds that sampling for diversity can raise hallucination rates.
Fluent is not the same as checked.

facts.claim: A 2023 survey splits LLM hallucination into factuality hallucination (output diverges from verifiable real-world facts) and faithfulness hallucination (output diverges from the user's input or is internally inconsistent)
facts.note: arXiv 2311.05232: factuality (factual contradiction, fabrication) vs faithfulness (instruction, context, logical inconsistency)

facts.claim: The same survey lists causes in data (misinformation, biases, knowledge boundaries), training (objectives, fine-tuning on knowledge the model lacks, sycophancy) and inference (decoding, over-confidence)
An earlier survey notes that sampling strategies that increase diversity can raise hallucination rates
facts.note: arXiv 2202.03629 (Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation): decoders and diversity-increasing sampling strategies can raise hallucination rates
